name: Whitening toothpaste

lead: Whitening toothpaste uses mild abrasives, stain-loosening chemicals and, in some products, peroxide or a blue pigment to make teeth look lighter. The payoff is a brighter smile as coffee and tea stains lift, at far lower cost than professional bleaching.

The effect is mostly mechanical and chemical removal of surface stains, with some products adding optical pigments. Wikipedia reports daily use typically takes two to four weeks to show, and a 2017 systematic review found nearly all whitening toothpastes reduced surface stain without changing the natural colour of the tooth. A 2025 randomised crossover trial looked at blue covarine toothpastes.

paras: People swap it in for regular toothpaste and brush twice daily, often alongside whitening strips or professional treatment. Results show over a few weeks and fade if use stops.
Highly abrasive formulas (measured as RDA) can wear enamel with excessive use, and peroxide products can demineralise teeth at high concentrations. Sensitivity can occur.

angle.text: Whitening toothpaste lifts surface stains from coffee and tea for a brighter-looking smile within weeks. It lightens surface stain rather than the tooth's natural shade, and costs far less than professional bleaching.

lead: Whitening toothpaste is toothpaste marketed to make teeth look lighter, using mild abrasives, chemical stain-loosening agents, in some products low levels of peroxide, or optical agents such as blue covarine [1][2][3]. It is sold over the counter at low cost and is the most accessible entry point to the wider set of whitening options, which also include strips, rinses, trays and professional bleaching [3].

People use it to lift the surface stains from coffee, tea, red wine and tobacco that dull a smile. A lighter, cleaner-looking smile is among the most visible parts of facial presentation, and daily whitening toothpaste is a routine way to maintain it between or after other treatments. Wikipedia reports that twice-daily use typically takes two to four weeks to produce visible lightening [1].

Reference sources generally describe the effect as removal or masking of surface (extrinsic) stains rather than a change in the natural tooth colour [1]. A 2017 systematic review, as summarised by Wikipedia, found that nearly all whitening dentifrices reduced extrinsic stain, whether or not they contained a chemical whitening agent [1]. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article says toothpastes can lighten teeth by one or two shades with continued use [3]. A 2025 randomised crossover trial examined blue covarine toothpastes and tooth colour [4].

About 2 to 4 weeks of twice-daily use [1]
One or two shades with continued use [3]
Relative dentin abrasivity (RDA); under 250 regarded as safe for lifelong use by ANSI and the ADA [1]

paras: Abrasion is the main way any toothpaste removes stain, and abrasives make up roughly 8 to 20 percent of a typical formula [1]. Whitening formulas may add polishing agents to lift stain more effectively [1]. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article says whitening toothpastes contain more abrasives and detergents than regular ones and that some include low levels of carbamide or hydrogen peroxide, but not sodium hypochlorite bleach [3]. Silica is a commonly used abrasive, and baking soda is described as a low-abrasive option that buffers acid and has shown no reported adverse effects in clinical studies [3].

Chemical agents such as sodium tripolyphosphate are used to break down or dissolve stain without relying on scrubbing [1]. Blue covarine products deposit a thin blue pigment intended to shift the apparent colour of the tooth surface toward white [4]. Mica is sometimes added to toothpaste as a mild abrasive and for a cosmetic shimmer [1]. Some toothpastes contain hydroxyapatite, a mineral form of tooth enamel studied mainly for caries prevention [5][6].

Charcoal has been added to some toothpastes. Wikipedia reports that the American Dental Association does not recommend charcoal toothpaste and that evidence on its safety and effectiveness is lacking [1].

A review of natural whitening explains that substances from tea, coffee, food dyes and tobacco smoke, as well as antibiotics such as tetracycline, can percolate into the porous structure of enamel, and that ageing exposes yellow dentin as enamel wears [2]. Surface stains respond to polishing and chemical lifting; deeper intrinsic discolouration is the target of peroxide bleaching [1][3]. Wikipedia notes that bleaching tends to work least well on grey teeth and on tetracycline staining, which can need prolonged treatment [3].

Toothpaste is reported to remove surface stains and not to reverse discolouration from within the tooth [1]. Wikipedia's whitening article describes toothpastes as lightening teeth by one or two shades with continued use. By comparison, strips used twice daily for 14 days give a similar change within several days, trays can show results in about three days, and in-office bleaching can lift shade by 2 to 7 shades [3].

A review of natural whitening approaches states that high-concentration peroxide whiteners can deproteinize and demineralize teeth through oxidation if used excessively, while describing natural ingredients as lightening teeth without eroding surfaces [2]. An in situ randomised study compared the whitening effect of different toothpastes on bovine enamel [7].

sections.h: Whitening toothpaste within the wider whitening toolkit
paras: Whitening toothpaste is usually positioned as a low-intensity, daily option. Peroxide gels in trays, strips and rinses act by releasing free radicals that break pigment molecules into smaller ones that reflect less light, while peroxyacid products are described as an alternative route that avoids free radical formation [3]. Wikipedia reports that light activation of in-office gels has not been shown to improve results clearly [3].

Wikipedia also notes that a large share of the colour change from an intensive in-office session can fade within the first week, largely through tooth rehydration, which is one reason some people follow professional treatment with maintenance products such as whitening toothpaste [3].

Abrasive toothpastes are rated by relative dentin abrasivity; a value below 250 is considered safe for lifelong use by ANSI and the ADA according to Wikipedia, and values above that may damage tooth surfaces [1]. Wikipedia describes whitening toothpaste as generally safe for daily use, while noting that excessive use may damage enamel [1].

Sensitivity is the main side effect of whitening products in general; potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride in toothpastes can ease it [3]. Peroxide products can also irritate gums, and Wikipedia reports that sensitivity after in-office hydrogen peroxide treatment has been recorded in roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of patients [3]. Wikipedia also describes "bleachorexia", an obsessive pattern of repeated whitening that resembles body dysmorphic disorder [3].

A Cochrane review separately examines fluoride toothpaste for caries prevention, and an 18-month trial compared a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste with 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste in adults [8][5]. Wikipedia reports that the 2019 Cochrane review found concentrations below 1,000 ppm unlikely to prevent decay [1].

In the EU, retail whitening products are limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6% allowed only under professional supervision to patients aged 18 or older; the US FDA endorses gels under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide, according to Wikipedia [3]. The same source says more than 100 million Americans whiten their teeth, spending about $15 billion in 2010 [3]. In the UK, the General Dental Council raised concerns in 2010 about unsafe whitening by untrained staff [3].

Tooth powders date back to ancient Egypt, and Colgate began mass-producing aromatic toothpaste in jars in 1873, with collapsible tubes arriving in 1880 [1]. Fluoride was first added to toothpastes in the 1890s according to Wikipedia, and Crest launched a clinically tested fluoride toothpaste in 1955 [1]. Grokipedia gives 1956 for the introduction of fluoride to toothpaste [9].

On the whitening side, Wikipedia dates custom-tray bleaching to the late 1960s, introduced by Dr William Klusmeier, with Haywood and Heymann supporting the method in 1989, and over-the-counter strips to the late 1980s [3]. Earlier whitening attempts included acids and filing by 17th-century barbers, oxalic acid in 1877 and calcium hypochlorite [3]. Whitening toothpastes grew out of this long history of abrasive dentifrices.

Discussion on looksmax.org touches on toothpaste mainly through fluoride safety: one thread debated whether fluoride-free "natural" toothpaste gives any protection against decay, with a poster arguing that dentists dissuade patients from fluoride-free products [10].

Randomised studies include a crossover trial of blue covarine toothpastes and tooth colour [4] and an in situ trial of whitening toothpastes on bovine enamel [7]. Abstract details for these were limited, so effect sizes are not reported here. A 2017 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found nearly all whitening dentifrices reduced extrinsic stain [1]. Large trials of toothpaste more broadly concern caries prevention: a Cochrane network meta-analysis examined fluoride concentrations [8], an updated systematic review and meta-analysis examined hydroxyapatite and caries [6], and an 18-month double-blinded equivalence trial compared hydroxyapatite and 1450 ppm fluoride toothpastes using DMFS as the endpoint [5].

lore.intro: Toothpaste appears on looksmax.org mostly in discussions of fluoride safety rather than whitening [10]. Whitening claims around toothpaste are largely those made by manufacturers and users in general consumer settings.
